analysis.one_liner: Caps child care costs at 7% of income for low- and moderate-income families and expands preschool and Head Start.
analysis.headline: The Child Care for Working Families Act — a bill capping child care costs at 7% of family income, backed by 106 House cosponsors, all Democrats — never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Child Care for Working Families Act would have capped what low- and moderate-income families pay for child care on a sliding scale — families under 75% of their state's median income would pay nothing, and no subsidized family would pay more than 7% of its income. Starting in October 2024, every eligible child in a participating state would be guaranteed a child care slot, rather than today's system where eligible families end up on waiting lists. The bill also funded state preschool for three- to five-year-olds, expanded Head Start to full-day and full-year service, required child care staff to be paid a living wage comparable to elementary educators, and paid for building new providers in underserved areas. It was authorized at $20 billion in its first year, rising to $40 billion, with open-ended funding after that.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income families with young children: copayments would be eliminated below 75% of state median income and capped at 7% of income for everyone receiving assistance, and from October 2024 every eligible child would be guaranteed a slot rather than a place on a waiting list. Child care workers, who are among the lowest-paid members of the workforce, would be guaranteed at least a living wage and pay comparable to elementary educators with similar credentials. Providers in underserved communities would get startup grants, facility funding, and higher payment rates based on actual costs. Head Start agencies would get funding to serve children full-day and full-year and to raise staff pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and moderate-income families with young children

how_it_helps.text: Caps what a subsidized family pays for child care on a sliding scale: families below 75% of their state's median income pay nothing, and no participating family pays more than 7% of household income.

Beginning October 1, 2024, every eligible child whose family applies in a participating state must be offered assistance — converting today's waitlisted, limited program into an entitlement for all eligible children.

Requires states to set provider payment rates from a cost-estimation model and to ensure child care staff earn at least a living wage and wages comparable to elementary educators with similar credentials, with a wage ladder written into every state plan.

Establishes grants for states to create free or low-cost preschool programs for low- and moderate-income three- to five-year-olds, and funds Head Start agencies to offer full-day, full-year services and pay staff a living wage.

Directs a large share of funding to building supply in underserved communities — startup grants, facility construction in 2022-2024, and priority slots for children with disabilities, homeless children, and children in foster care.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through appropriations of $20 billion in fiscal 2022, $30 billion in fiscal 2023, and $40 billion in fiscal 2024, then such sums as necessary each year after — with no specified offset or pay-for in the bill. Some small and informal providers would bear the cost of meeting new quality standards and wage floors, though the bill provides grants to help them comply.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $20 billion for fiscal 2022, $30 billion for fiscal 2023, and $40 billion for fiscal 2024, then such sums as may be necessary every year after — a large, permanent federal commitment that would either add to deficits or require tax increases or offsets.

Providers receiving subsidized children would have to meet a tiered quality system with national or evidence-based standards, and their staff would have to be paid at least a living wage and wages comparable to elementary educators with similar credentials — requirements that raise operating costs and could push some small or informal family, friend, and neighbor providers out of the subsidized system, though the bill creates a separate, lighter set of standards for that type of care and startup and improvement grants to help providers comply.

Because assistance flows through state agencies and private providers, states would need several years to build the required cost-estimation models, quality-rating systems, and equity reviews before the guarantee of assistance for every eligible child takes effect in October 2024, meaning families would not see the full benefit immediately.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for families are large and well-targeted: child care is one of the biggest household expenses for working parents, and the bill directly caps what families pay while raising what workers earn and expanding supply. The costs are real and honest supporters had to own them: $20 billion growing to $40 billion a year and then an open-ended federal entitlement is a major permanent commitment of taxpayer money, and the wage and quality requirements would force some small and informal providers to close or go through difficult transitions. The bill would also lock in private providers as the delivery channel for a heavily subsidized public service, which adds administrative complexity. On balance, for the families it covers, the benefits clearly outweigh the costs; the genuine disagreement was over the federal price tag and delivery design, not over whether the underlying problem is real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2021, sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, and sat there — no markup, no floor vote — until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott introduced the bill on April 22, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 117th Congress.
It gathered 106 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat; no Republican signed on.
The bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023, and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything new from the bill's death. Working families continue to pay full market child care costs, child care workers continue at low wages, and the federal government avoids the $20-40 billion per year commitment the bill would have made.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one gained; families keep paying full price

for.name: Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott
for.role: U.S. Representative (VA-3); Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee, the House Committee on Education and Labor, which took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

for.name: 106 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican signed on.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — all 106 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsored — but there was never a vote in either chamber, so no recorded party split exists on the merits.

industries.note: Federal appropriations of $20-40 billion a year would flow to providers through higher payment rates, startup and quality-improvement grants, and facility funding, while wages for their staff rise to a living wage and educator-comparable levels. Their interest runs alongside families': better-paid, better-funded providers mean more and better care, though quality standards impose new compliance costs.
The bill funds full-school-day and full-year Head Start services, additional hours for migrant and seasonal programs, and requires HHS to help agencies pay teachers and staff a living wage.

industries.industry: Informal family, friend, and neighbor caregivers
industries.note: Most of these caregivers would be placed under a separate, lighter set of quality standards rather than the full tiered system, and could receive training, grants, and help getting licensed. But joining the subsidized system would still bring requirements that some informal providers may choose to forgo.
